primary_topics: Address at a two-day Asian constitutional courts conference, November 29, 2006 -- one week before CJP's retirement; the Philippines has no separate constitutional court, the SC discharges all constitutional court functions
The twin-standard framework for Asian constitutional courts: strict scrutiny for civil and political rights; deferential stance for economic and development rights

The Global Forum on Liberty and Prosperity (October 18-20, 2006) as the governing event: unanimity on pursuing both liberty and prosperity; the caveat that each country must pursue its own philosophical and jurisprudential identity
The governing balance: 'finding the right balance is indeed a country-to-country search depending on the history, culture, environment, habits and mores in each jurisdiction'
sub_topics: Philippines' unique constitutional structure: unlike the countries attending the conference, the Philippines has no separate constitutional court; 'its functions and duties are discharged by our Supreme Court'

Historical context: 'our history shows that civil and political rights, particularly those enshrined in our Bill of Rights, have been zealously guarded and upheld. Courts are expected to safeguard liberty. Their role is to be the great equalizers when individual freedoms are buffeted by the awesome powers of the State.'
Economic rights equally constitutional: Article on Principles and State Policies (just and dynamic social order); Article XII (equitable distribution of opportunities, income and wealth)

Two standards of review: (1) strict scrutiny for liberty cases -- 'scales of justice have weighed heavily against government and in favor of the people, especially the poor, the oppressed, the marginalized, the dispossessed and the weak. Laws and actions of government come to the court highly suspect in their constitutional validity, whenever they restrict the fundamental rights of our people'; (2) deferential interpretation for prosperity cases -- 'deference is accorded to the political branches of government, namely the Presidency and Congress'

Global Forum on Liberty and Prosperity: hosted by the SC October 18-20, 2006; 'unanimity on the need to pursue both liberty and prosperity'; the caveat: 'each country must pursue internally its own quest for its own philosophical and jurisprudential identity'

Philippine formula: 'the peculiar facts and distinct circumstances of the Philippines make the formula Liberty and Prosperity still the most viable economic and judicial philosophy here. After all, during the years of Martial Law, authoritarian rule was proven to be incapable of producing meaningful long-term economic progress.'

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered November 29, 2006 at a two-day Asian constitutional courts conference -- one week before CJP's mandatory retirement -- this address presents the liberty-and-prosperity twin-standard framework to an international judicial audience. CJP opens with a structural clarification: unlike the other countries attending, the Philippines has no separate constitutional court; the SC discharges all constitutional court functions. He presents the historical context (Philippine Bill of Rights zealously guarded; courts as great equalizers against State power) and the constitutional economic rights mandate (just and dynamic social order; equitable distribution of opportunities, income and wealth). He describes the two standards of review: (1) strict scrutiny for civil and political rights -- 'scales of justice have weighed heavily against government and in favor of the people, especially the poor, the oppressed, the marginalized, the dispossessed and the weak'; (2) deferential stance for prosperity and development issues -- 'deference is accorded to the political branches of government, namely the Presidency and Congress.' The October 18-20, 2006 Global Forum on Liberty and Prosperity provided the governing international evidence: 'unanimity on the need to pursue both liberty and prosperity'; but also the caveat that 'each country must pursue internally its own quest for its own philosophical and jurisprudential identity.' Philippines-specific conclusion: 'the peculiar facts and distinct circumstances of the Philippines make the formula Liberty and Prosperity still the most viable economic and judicial philosophy here. After all, during the years of Martial Law, authoritarian rule was proven to be incapable of producing meaningful long-term economic progress.' Closing: 'I wish the Asian constitutional courts good speed and success in finding and striking the right balance between the sometimes contending demands and jurisdictions of the state, culture and religion; and, if I may add, those of safeguarding the liberty and nurturing the prosperity of our peoples.'
